horseshoe

No open copy of this paper was found: only its title is stored. It needs a Zotero copy to be read in.

How it connects

  • Empirical Bayes normal means uses this
    The framework includes the horseshoe prior for sparse signals.
    “Another parametric prior that is well suited for capturing sparse signals is the horseshoe prior, which models sparsity by having appreciable mass near zero rather than exactly at zero (Carvalho, Polson, and Scott 2010).”
    Empirical Bayes normal means · ebnm.txt | Sparse priors (citation sentence)
  • is a special case of SMoothing by Adaptive SHrinkage (component)
    The prior family includes the horseshoe distribution as a special case.
    “This family includes, as a special case, the distributions used in Clyde and George (2000), Johnstone and Silverman (2005b), and many others (Carvalho et al., 2010, e.g., the Horseshoe prior of).”
    SMoothing by Adaptive SHrinkage · smash.txt | 2.1 Empirical Bayes Shrinkage (citation sentence)
  • is a special case of Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) (component) when The shrinkage distribution has beta parameters one-half and one-half and phi equals one.
    The horseshoe prior is the stated special case with phi equal to one.
    “A special case where φ = 1 leads to ρj ~ (1/2, 1/2) (beta distribution) where the name of the prior arises, horseshoe (HS) [6, 7].”
    Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) · tpb.txt | 2 Background (citation sentence)
  • Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) (component) extends this
    The proposed prior family simultaneously extends the cited normal-gamma and horseshoe constructions.
    “It provides a rich class of priors leading to great flexibility in terms of the induced shrinkage and makes it clear that this new class of priors can be considered simultaneous extensions to the work by [11, 12] and [6, 7].”
    Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) · tpb.txt | Proposition 1 (citation sentence)
  • Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) (component) extends this
    The proposed hierarchy expresses the horseshoe hierarchy in a conjugate form.
    “The aforementioned observation helps us formulate the complete hierarchy proposed in [7] in a conjugate manner.”
    Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) · tpb.txt | Corollary 1 (citation sentence)
  • is a special case of Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) (component) when Different treatments of higher-level hyperparameters are disregarded.
    The proposed prior family unifies the cited priors through equivalent hierarchies.
    “Hence disregarding the different treatments of the higher-level hyper-parameters, we have shown that the class of priors given in Definition 2 unites the priors in [16, 11, 6, 7] under one family and reveals their close connections through the equivalence of hierarchies given in Proposition 1.”
    Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) · tpb.txt | Corollary 2 (citation sentence)
  • Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) (component) uses this
    The global-scale hierarchy uses the same half-Cauchy construction as the horseshoe prior.
    “Thus we follow the hierarchy by letting φ ~ (1/2, ω), ω ~ (1/2, 1) which implies φ1/2 ~ (0, 1) that is identical to what was used in [7] at this level of the hierarchy.”
    Three-parameter beta normal scale mixtures (TPBN) · tpb.txt | 4.1 Fully Bayes and Approximate Inference (citation sentence)
  • PRS-CS (prior) can be derived from this when a = b = 1/2 within the gamma-gamma/TPB prior family.
    The gamma-gamma/TPB prior family discussed for PRS-CS yields the horseshoe prior when a and b both equal one half.
    “It can be seen that when a = 1/2 and b = 1/2, the TPB prior has substantial mass near zero and one (Fig. 3, upper panel), and thus the corresponding prior density on βj has a very sharp peak around the origin, with zero being a pole (singular point; Fig. 3, middle panel), along with heavy, Cauchy-like tails (Fig. 3, lower panel). This prior is known as the horseshoe prior50, due to the horseshoe-shaped prior density on the shrinkage factor τj.”
    PRS-CS · prscs.txt | line 69 | prscs | journal OA version (PMC6467998) | Methods > PRS-CS and PRS-CS-auto

empirical Bayes

A generic statistical tool. It has no paper of its own on this map: each link below is a sentence from the paper that says it uses it.

How it connects

  • Sum of Single Effects regression (SuSiE) (inference algorithm) uses this when Version with estimated component prior variances.
    The empirical Bayes version of SuSiE estimates the prior variances, effectively estimating the number of effects.
    “While inferences are generally robust to overstating L, we also note that the Empirical Bayes version of our method, which estimates σ_{0}^{2}, also effectively estimates the number of effects: when L is greater than the number of signals in the data, the maximum likelihood estimate of σ_{0 l}^{2} will be zero or close to zero for many l, which in turn forces bl to zero.”
    Sum of Single Effects regression (SuSiE) · susie | PMC author manuscript | Choice of L
  • fSuSiE (inference algorithm) uses this
    The prior and noise parameters are estimated by an empirical Bayes marginal-likelihood approach.
    “We adopt an Empirical Bayes (EB) approach, by first estimating our prior g and the noise parameters θ by maximizing the marginal log-likelihood:”
    fSuSiE · fsusie | PMC-hosted bioRxiv v1 (2025-08-17) | Derivation of the fSuSiE model fitting algorithms
  • Adaptive shrinkage (ash) (inference algorithm) uses this when Usual two-step fit; ash modifies the hyperparameter objective with a penalty.
    Ash estimates mixture hyperparameters from the likelihood and plugs them into conditional effect posteriors.
    “The usual EB approach to fitting this model would involve two steps: 1. Estimate the hyper-parameters }{}$\pi$ by maximizing the likelihood }{}$L(\pi)$ , given by (2.5), yielding }{}$\hat{\pi} := \arg \max L(\pi)$ .2. Compute quantities of interest from the conditional distributions }{}$p(\beta_j | \hat{\beta}, \hat{s}, \hat{\pi})$ . For example, the evidence against the null hypothesis }{}$\beta_j=0$ can be summarized by }{}$p(\beta_j \neq 0 | \hat{\beta}, \hat{s},\hat{\pi})$ .”
    Adaptive shrinkage (ash) · ash | journal OA version, PMC5379932 | 2.2. Fitting the model
  • Multivariate adaptive shrinkage uses this
    Mash uses empirical Bayes hierarchical modeling.
    “The mash method uses EB hierarchical modelling, and so is related to other EB methods5,6,12.”
    Multivariate adaptive shrinkage · mash | PMC author manuscript | Discussion
  • Sum of Shared Single Effects (SuShiE) (inference algorithm) uses this
    SuShiE learns residual variances and prior effect covariance matrices by an Empirical Bayes-like ELBO-maximization procedure.
    “We use an Empirical Bayes-like procedure to infer our hyperparameters: environmental/residual variance σ_{i , e}^{2} ( i = 1 , … , k ) and cis-molQTL effect size covariance matrices across ancestries C_{l} ( l = 1 , … , L ) by directly maximize the ELBO54. As reflected in algorithms 1 and 2 in Supplementary Note 1, inference alternates between inferring variational parameters while keeping hyperparameters fixed (e.g., C_{l} and σ_{i , e}^{2}), and inferring hyperparameters while keeping variational parameters fixed (e.g., μ_{l , j} , Σ_{l , j}, and α_{l}), which is akin to a coordinate ascent procedure that includes both variational- and hyper-parameters54.”
    Sum of Shared Single Effects (SuShiE) · sushie | PMC12767540 author manuscript | Methods > Inferring hyperparameters

mixture model

A generic statistical tool. It has no paper of its own on this map: each link below is a sentence from the paper that says it uses it.

How it connects

  • Adaptive shrinkage (ash) (prior) uses this when Pre-specified components; weights nonnegative and summing to one.
    Ash represents the prior as a point mass at zero and a mixture of fixed component distributions.
    “where f0 is a point mass on 0, and fk (k = 1, . . . , K) are pre-specified component distributions with one of the following forms: (i) fk (·) = N (·; 0, σk2 ), (“ash.n”) (ii) fk (·) = U [·; −ak , ak ], (“ash.u”) (iii) fk (·) = U [·; −ak , 0] and/or U [·; 0, ak ], (“ash.hu”) where U [·; a, b] denotes the density of a uniform distribution on [a, b]. (In (iii) we include both components in the mixture (S.1.1), so a grid of values a1 , . . . , aK defines 2K + 1 mixture com- ponent densities, and π is a 2K + 1 vector that sums to 1.)”
    Adaptive shrinkage (ash) · ash | journal OA version, PMC5379932 supplement kxw041_Supp.pdf | S.1 Model Embellishment Details > More flexible unimodal distributions
  • Multivariate Sum of Single Effects (mvSuSiE) (prior) uses this
    The single-effect prior is a flexible mixture of normal distributions.
    “In summary, mvSuSiE is a multivariate regression model with a flexible mixture-of-normals prior on the ‘single effects’”
    Multivariate Sum of Single Effects (mvSuSiE) · mvsusie | PMC12900646.1 journal OA version (2026-02-03) | The mvSuSiE model
  • Wavelet-based genetic association analysis (prior) uses this when Conditional on fitted pi under the stated hierarchical model.
    Given fitted scale proportions, effect posteriors are mixtures of a point mass at zero and a three-parameter t distribution.
    “Under the above hierarchical model, given π̂, the posterior distributions on the effect sizes in the wavelet space, p(βsl |y, g, π̂), are available in closed form. Specifically, the βsl are a posteriori independent, each having a distribution that is a mixture of a point mass at zero and a three parameter version of a t distribution [Jackman (2009)], with density given in Supplementary Material [Shim and Stephens (2015)].”
    Wavelet-based genetic association analysis · wavelet_ss | PMC author manuscript (PMC5795621) | 3.5. Effect size estimates

How it connects

  • fSuSiE (prior) extends this
    The SPS prior extends a scale-dependent spike-and-slab prior to a normal-mixture prior.
    “Previous wavelet regression approaches have exploited the scale-dependent sparsity of the wavelet coefficients [49, 82] [95, 96]. One of these approaches used a spike-and-slab prior [95, 96]. Building on this spike-and-slab prior as well as our recent work on adaptive shrinkage methods [81] [97, 98], we extend this scale-dependent spike-and-slab prior to a scale-dependent mixture prior, which we refer to as the “shrinkage-per-scale” (SPS) prior: g_{s l}^{r} = ∑ k = 0 K π_{k s}^{r} N 0 , σ_{k s}^{2} . (12)”
    fSuSiE · fsusie | PMC-hosted bioRxiv v1 (2025-08-17) | Scale-dependent mixture priors for fSuSiE
  • Bayesian variable selection regression (prior) uses this
    The sparse BVSR formulation uses a point-mass-at-zero and normal-mixture effect prior.
    “Some formulations of BVSR use a similar “sparse” prior, where the marginal prior on \beta_{j} βj\beta_{j} is a mixture of a point mass at 0 and a normal distribution,”
    Bayesian variable selection regression · bvsr | arXiv:1110.6019v1 (2011-10-27) | 2 Models and priors

    The non-infinitesimal prior uses a zero spike and Gaussian slab.

XTX = nΦ; here, Φ is the pairwise genotypic covariance, which can be estimated from a reference panel representative of the population used in the GWAS.   • mvSuSiE with regression summary statistics (data input) uses this when Centered and standardized X and Y; in-sample LD for exact recovery

  • LDpred (data input) uses this when Standardized marginal effects; signed Z/sqrt(N) approximation when needed
    LDpred uses marginal least-squares marker effects from the additive phenotype model.
    “We model the phenotype as a linear combination of M genetic effects and an independent environmental effect $\epsilon $, i.e., $Y={\sum }_{i=1}^{M}{X}_{i}{\beta }_{i}+\epsilon $, where ${X}_{i}$ denotes the i^{th} genetic variant, ${\beta }_{i}$ is its true effect, and $\epsilon $ is the environmental and noise contribution. In this setting, the (marginal) least-squares estimate of an individual marker effect is ${\stackrel{ˆ}{\beta }}_{i}={X}_{i}^{\prime }Y/N$.”

    “We first note that, given variance parameters σ2, ϕ and ψj, j = 1,2,…, M, and the marginal least squares effect size estimates of the regression coefficients β ^ = Z^{T} y ∕ N, the posterior mean of β is”
    PRS-CS · prscs | journal OA version (PMC6467998) | Methods > PRS-CS and PRS-CS-auto
  • PRS-CSx (data input) uses this when Given variance parameters sigma_k^2, phi and psi_j.
    PRS-CSx uses marginal least-squares SNP effect estimates with population-specific LD in its conditional posterior mean.
    “More specifically, given the variance parameters σ_{k}^{2}, ϕ and Ψj, and the marginal least squares estimates of the SNP effect sizes in population k, β ^_{k} = X_{k}^{T} y_{k} / N_{k}, the posterior mean of βk is E [ β_{k} | β ^_{k} ] = ( D_{k} + Ψ^{− 1} )^{− 1} β ^_{k}, where D_{k} = X_{k}^{T} X_{k} / N_{k} is the LD matrix for population k, and Ψ = diag{Ψ1, Ψ2, ⋯ ,ΨM} is a diagonal matrix (Supplementary Note).”

How it connects

  • fSuSiE (model likelihood) uses this
    The elementary Bayesian functional regression building block is a Gaussian linear model with independent normal effect priors.
    “The most basic building block in our derivations is a wavelet regression model in which the effects have independent normal priors. We call this the simple Bayesian functional regression model: D = xf ⊺ + E eit ∼ N (0, σ 2 ) (23) fs,l ∼ N (0, σ02 ),”
    fSuSiE · fsusie | PMC-hosted bioRxiv v1 (2025-08-17) | Simple Bayesian functional regression
  • BridgePRS (model likelihood) uses this
    The locus model uses a Gaussian linear trait likelihood with a multivariate Gaussian SNP-effect prior.
    “Within loci, SNP effect sizes β are modeled by a multivariate Gaussian distribution, and we assume that the trait y of individuals with genotype data X at the locus follows a Gaussian distribution y ~ N(Xβ, ψI). Throughout, the Gaussian distribution is parameterized by its mean and precision matrix (inverse covariance matrix).”
    BridgePRS · bridgeprs | journal OA version | Methods > The BridgePRS model
  • PRS-CS (model likelihood) uses this
    PRS-CS uses a Bayesian high-dimensional regression model for polygenic prediction.
    “We consider a Bayesian high-dimensional regression framework for polygenic modeling and prediction:”
    PRS-CS · prscs | journal OA version (PMC6467998) | Results > Conceptual frameworks
  • PRS-CSx (model likelihood) uses this when Standardized phenotypes and genotypes; population-specific Gaussian isotropic residuals.
    PRS-CSx uses a population-specific Bayesian high-dimensional linear regression model.
    “Consider the following Bayesian high-dimensional linear regression model for K populations: y_{k} = X_{k} β_{k} + ϵ_{k} , ϵ_{k} ~ MVN ( 0 , σ_{k}^{2} I ) , π ( σ_{k}^{2} ) ∝ σ_{k}^{− 2} , k = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , K , where, for each population k, yk is a vector of standardized phenotypes (zero mean and unit variance) from Nk individuals, Xk is an Nk × Mk matrix of standardized genotypes (each column has zero mean and unit variance), βk is a vector of SNP effect sizes, ϵk is a vector of normally distributed non-genetic effects with variance σ_{k}^{2}, for which we assign a non-informative scale-invariant Jeffreys prior, and I is an identify matrix.”
    PRS-CSx · prscsx | PMC author manuscript (PMC9117455) | METHODS > PRS-CSx

global-local shrinkage

A generic statistical tool. It has no paper of its own on this map: each link below is a sentence from the paper that says it uses it.

How it connects

  • PRS-CS (prior) uses this
    PRS-CS combines a shared global scale with marker-specific local scales.
    “β_{j} ~ N 0 , (σ^{2})/(N) ϕ ψ_{j} , ψ_{j} ~ g , 6 where the variance of βj scales with the residual variance and the sample size, ϕ is a global scaling parameter that is shared across all effect sizes, ψj is a local, marker-specific parameter, and g is an absolutely continuous mixing density function. This type of prior is known as global-local scale mixtures of normals.”
    PRS-CS · prscs | journal OA version (PMC6467998) | Methods > PRS-CS and PRS-CS-auto
  • PRS-CSx (prior) uses this
    PRS-CSx uses global-local shrinkage with a global sparsity parameter and SNP-specific local scales.
    “For SNP j in population k, we place a continuous shrinkage prior on its effect size βjk, which can be represented as global-local scale mixtures of normals: β_{j k} ~ N ( 0 , (σ_{k}^{2})/(N_{k}) ψ_{j} ) , ψ_{j} ~ Gamma ( a , δ_{j} ) , δ_{j} ~ Gamma ( b , ϕ ) , where ϕ is a global shrinkage parameter shared across all SNPs that models the overall sparseness of the genetic architecture, and Ψj is a local, SNP-specific shrinkage parameter that is adaptive to marginal GWAS associations. By assigning a gamma-gamma hierarchical prior on Ψj (specifically, the Strawderman-Berger prior with a = 1 and b = 1/2 in this work), the marginal prior density of βjk has sizable amount of mass near zero to impose strong shrinkage on small noisy signals, and in the meantime, heavy Cauchy-like tails to avoid over-shrinkage of truly non-zero effects.”
    PRS-CSx · prscsx | PMC author manuscript (PMC9117455) | METHODS > PRS-CSx

Enter allelic, dominance, and interlocus interaction terms in sequence; select extra terms by improvement in AIC
Reports
Disease-risk predictions on an odds/log-odds scale
Data
Individual SNP genotypes encoded as allele counts 0/1/2, dominance indicators, and interlocus interaction terms
You set
Choice of included terms via AIC; alternative link-scale assessment profiles rho in the power-of-odds family

How it connects

Detached on purpose: no passage in the stored paper names this method together with another method on the map, so no link is drawn.

Stated limits 1
  • The logistic model has no simple biological interpretation and its quantitative interactions rarely have a biological interpretation.
What the authors say about other methods 3
  • The power-of-odds link family contains the multiplicative model at rho = 0 and the additive model at rho = 1, and is fitted over rho using a log-likelihood profile.
  • The additive risk model approximately corresponds to independent sufficient causes, but rejecting that potentially implausible model may provide limited etiological insight.
  • Under Good’s maximum-entropy construction, the null hypothesis is no logistic-regression interaction, equating the resulting information synergy with logistic interaction.

linear mixed model

STATO:0000464 · a term of the STATO statistics ontology

STATO definition

A lnear mixed model is a mixed model containing both fixed effects and random effects and in which factors and covariates are assumed to have a linear relationship to the dependent variable. These models are useful in a wide variety of disciplines in the physical, biological and social sciences. They are particularly useful in settings where repeated measurements are made on the same statistical units (longitudinal study), or where measurements are made on clusters of related statistical units. Because of their advantage in dealing with missing values, mixed effects models are often preferred over more traditional approaches such as repeated measures ANOVA. Fixed-effects factors are generally considered to be the variables whose values of interest are all represented in the data file. Random-effects factors are variables whose values correspond to unwanted variation. They are useful when trying to understand variability in the dependent variable which was not anticipated and exceeds what was expected. Linear mixed models also allow to specify specific interactions between factors, and allow the evaluation of the various linear effect that a particular combination of factor levels may have on a response variable. Finally, linear mixed models allow to specify variance components in order to describe the relation between various random effects levels.

STATO's source for this term

adapted from Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_model

credible interval

STATO:0000455 · a term of the STATO statistics ontology

STATO definition

In Bayesian statistics context, a credible interval is an interval of a posterior distribution which is such that the density at any point inside the interval is greater than the density at any point outside and that the area under the curve for that interval is equal to a prespecified probability level. For any probability level there is generally only one such interval, which is also often known as the highest posterior density region. Unlike the usual confidence interval associated with frequentist inference, here the intervals specify the range within which parameters lie with a certain probability. The Bayesian counterparts of the confidence interval used in Frequentists Statistics.

Adapted from Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credible_interval and from the Cambridge Dictionary of Statistics, fourth edition, ISBN-13 978-0-511-78827-7 last accessed: 2017-07-01

false discovery rate correction method

OBI:0200163 · a term of the STATO statistics ontology

STATO definition

The false discovery rate is a data transformation used in multiple hypothesis testing to correct for multiple comparisons. It controls the expected proportion of incorrectly rejected null hypotheses (type I errors) in a list of rejected hypotheses. It is a less conservative comparison procedure with greater power than familywise error rate (FWER) control, at a cost of increasing the likelihood of obtaining type I errors. .

Assumes 8
  • Coding a SNP by 0, 1 or 2 reference alleles assumes an additive genetic model.
  • Population structure is assumed to have been corrected before the BVSR analysis.
  • The nonzero regression coefficients have independent priors conditional on the model and hyperparameters.
  • The effects are exchangeable and all covariates are equally plausible candidates a priori.
  • Variables are included independently with a common probability pi.
  • Residual phenotypes are assumed normally distributed; marginal normal-quantile transformation does not strictly ensure residual normality.
  • The binary extension identifies the latent scale by constraining empirical latent variance to one.
  • The nonzero effect-size distribution is assumed normal.
Guarantees and stated results 4
  • In the stated diffuse-prior limit, relative model marginal likelihoods are invariant to shifting or scaling the phenotype. theorem
  • Centering the response and all covariates and fixing the intercept to zero yields the same inclusion-vector posterior as the limiting intercept prior. theorem
  • The expected relative signal variance conditional on gamma and sigma_a equals sigma_a^2 times the sum of selected covariate variances. theorem
  • The stated uniform-h transform Z=h/(1-h) has density 1/(1+z)^2 and yields a heavy-tailed scale prior. theorem
Stated limits 8
  • The simple MCMC scheme can perform poorly for multiple correlated covariates far apart on a chromosome that require careful joint inclusion updates.
  • The analysis does not aim to recover a single best or correct model in weak-signal p much greater than n settings.
  • Normally distributed effects can be inappropriate for phenotypes with unusually large-effect loci; heavier-tailed effects are suggested for robustness.
  • Independent inclusion priors ignore local clustering of functional variants and can be overly skeptical of multiple functional variants in one gene.
  • Genotyping error correlated with phenotype can generate false associations, and multi-SNP analyses can propagate low-quality SNP effects to other SNPs.
  • Retaining an improper precision prior in unconstrained latent probit BVSR yields improper precision and latent-variable posteriors.
  • For genome-wide binary data the authors report harder mixing than for quantitative traits and possible need for longer runs or methodological changes.
  • The presented approach does not aim to discover nonadditive SNP combinations whose effects lack marginal signal.
What the authors say about other methods 16
  • BVSR builds on standard normal multiple linear regression.
  • The sparse BVSR formulation uses a point-mass-at-zero and normal-mixture effect prior.
  • BVSR uses MCMC to sample its posterior over h, pi and gamma.
  • The joint hyperparameter and inclusion sampler is a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with local proposals.
  • BVSR compounds local moves into small-world proposals, which the authors state improve theoretical MCMC convergence rate.
  • Marginal-association-biased proposals are related to sure independence screening but retain positive proposal probability for every variable.
  • Rao-Blackwellization is used to reduce Monte Carlo variance in posterior summaries.
  • The conditional inclusion calculation amounts to univariate regression of residuals on one covariate.
  • Under orthogonal unit-variance covariates, the Liang g-prior parameter corresponds to n sigma_a^2.
  • Binary BVSR uses the latent-normal probit construction attributed to Albert and Chib.
  • The binary extension integrates latent variables with MCMC.
  • The marginal-likelihood expression used for collapsed BVSR computation is attributed to Servin and Stephens Protocol S1.
  • The selected-effect independent prior differs from Zellner g priors, which correlate coefficient priors according to covariate correlations.
  • Relative to LASSO and other penalized regressions, BVSR directly produces posterior probabilities of nonzero effects.
  • Rao-Blackwellized inclusion calculations are effectively single-SNP analyses controlling for SNPs currently in the model.
  • Unlike the point-mass-and-normal sparse prior, George and McCulloch use a mixture of two normals with different variances.

Where it sits in STATO

  • genetic association study broader
    association test for a functional phenotype
Assumes 3
  • The defined transform uses a region length B equal to a power of two.
  • The coefficient-level model assumes normally distributed residuals.
  • The hierarchical model assumes conditional independence of coefficients and effect sizes across scales and locations given pi.
Guarantees and stated results 3
  • The authors state that permutation p-values are valid under the null regardless of the correctness of the hierarchical modeling assumptions.
  • The authors state that quantile transformation guarantees the normal residual assumption under the null and consequently well-behaved null Bayes factors.
  • Linearity gives closed-form pointwise posterior means and variances for original-domain effects, although their full posterior has no simple analytic form.
Stated limits 4
  • The regression fails to incorporate the high sampling error of low-count coefficients, allowing them to add noise and reduce test power.
  • Permutation calibration does not remove the dependence assumption used in effect-shape estimation.
  • The Bayes-factor calculations based on normal-quantile-transformed data are not expected to work well for small sample sizes, and adequate sizes have not been determined.
  • Using only the first mapped base fails to capture splice-junction information carried by reads.
What the authors say about other methods 19
  • The method borrows wavelet-domain modeling ideas from functional mixed models because spatial effects can have sparse transformed representations.
  • The permutation implementation adapts the Besag-Clifford sequential procedure to avoid many permutations for nonsignificant results.
  • The authors contrast fixed-window tests with wavelet tests, arguing that the latter accommodate multiple scales and effects that change direction.
  • The method applies wavelet denoising to genotype effects on a signal rather than to the signal itself.
  • The authors borrow wavelet-domain modeling ideas from this functional mixed-model work.
  • The authors borrow wavelet-domain modeling ideas from this functional mixed-model work.
  • The method uses the Haar discrete wavelet transform.
  • The method applies wavelet denoising to estimate genotype effects on a signal.
  • The coefficient Bayes factor uses the models and priors from Servin and Stephens.
  • Each wavelet coefficient uses normal linear regression on one genotype covariate and an intercept.
  • The coefficient-level evidence uses a Bayes factor for association.
  • The maximum-likelihood estimate of the scale proportions is computed using EM.
  • The regional statistic is calibrated using independent random permutations of individuals.
  • The testing procedure follows the normal-quantile transformation idea attributed to van der Waerden.
  • The analysis uses principal components to adjust unmeasured confounding.
  • The workflow regresses transformed coefficients on principal components and uses the residuals.
  • The analysis reuses the four principal components used by Degner et al.
  • Given fitted scale proportions, effect posteriors are mixtures of a point mass at zero and a three-parameter t distribution.
  • The analysis uses qvalue to estimate FDR from site-level p-values.

9 Adaptive shrinkage (ash)

Built on Normal Means model. What is new: unimodal mixture prior.

The problem it answers

  • Standard FDR pipelines can let poor-precision measurements inflate estimated FDR, motivating the use of effect estimates together with standard errors.
  • The method seeks to connect effect estimation and testing through sign-error probabilities because large-scale studies commonly emphasize testing alone.
  • A flexible sparsity-inducing effect distribution and unequal standard deviations are needed to extend conventional EB shrinkage.

What it is

Model
Independent normal effect-estimate likelihood conditional on estimated standard errors; optional conditional t approximation
Prior
Point mass at zero plus a fixed-grid mixture of zero-centered normals (ash.n), symmetric uniforms (ash.u), or half-uniforms (ash.hu); optional scaled-effects prior beta_j/s_hat_j^alpha ~ g
Fitting
Estimate mixture weights by penalized marginal likelihood using convex interior-point optimization or EM; compute conditional posterior mixtures analytically
Reports
Posterior effect distributions and intervals; local FDR; local false sign rate; subset-average sign-error rate and s-values
Data
Effect estimates and corresponding estimated standard errors; known degrees of freedom for t extension; z scores suffice for fitted g and lfsr at alpha=1
You set
Component family; finite component scale or endpoint grid and density; penalty lambda (default lambda_0=10, others 1); alpha specified or likelihood-tuned

Where it sits in STATO

  • mixture distribution related
    prior is a unimodal mixture
  • false discovery rate correction method related
    ash gives local false discovery and sign rates; STATO's term is a P-value correction
Assumes 9
  • Effects are independent draws from a unimodal distribution.
  • The normal-mixture prior assumes symmetry about zero.
  • The basic model assumes identically distributed effects whose distribution does not depend on their standard errors.
  • Conditional on true effects and estimated standard errors, measurement errors are independent and normally distributed with specified variances.
  • Using the stated conditional likelihood as a joint likelihood amounts to assuming that the standard-error distribution does not depend on the mixture weights.
  • The degrees of freedom used to estimate standard errors are assumed known and common across effects for simplicity.
  • Observation errors are Gaussian and their standard deviations are initially treated as known.
  • The underlying effects are independent and identically distributed from an unknown g belonging to a specified family G.
  • The selected prior family is symmetric and unimodal at zero.
Guarantees and stated results 6
  • The penalized mixture-weight optimization is convex and can be solved using interior-point methods.
  • The local false sign rate is at least the local false discovery rate.
  • Normal, symmetric-uniform and half-uniform mixtures can respectively approximate any normal scale mixture, any symmetric zero-unimodal distribution, and any zero-unimodal distribution arbitrarily accurately.
  • Fitted g and lfsr depend on the effect-standard-error pairs only through z scores, while effect-size intervals still require the original pairs.
  • Intervals from a posterior conditional on the observations remain valid Bayesian inferences for subsets selected using those observations.
  • Marginal likelihood optimization over the mixture weights is a convex optimization problem.
Stated limits 12
  • Normal mixtures enforce symmetry and cannot closely approximate some symmetric unimodal distributions with flat tops.
  • A t distribution for the standardized statistic does not imply the proposed conditional t likelihood because the former treats the standard error as random and the latter conditions on it.
  • Near-zero nonnull effects can be indistinguishable from exact nulls, so the data effectively bound plausible null fractions from above without providing a lower bound.
  • Independence and conditional independence are difficult to relax, and correlated tests can affect estimated FDRs.
  • Unaddressed confounding can induce many correlated tests and excessive rejections, potentially compromising FDR control.
  • At small sample sizes the normal likelihood is inadequate and a t likelihood only partially addresses unstable estimated standard errors.
  • The empirical Bayes fit substitutes a point estimate of g and does not account for uncertainty in g as a fully Bayesian analysis would.
  • Using two-number summaries and generic likelihood approximations may lose statistical efficiency compared with context-specific likelihood methods.
  • Without the penalty, half-uniform fits may concentrate near-zero mass on one side of zero and produce misleadingly small sign-error probabilities.
  • Null-fraction estimates can become slightly anti-conservative when unimodality fails in the authors’ bimodal simulation.
  • Uniform-mixture fits may curtail the tails of g and understate the probability of large outlying effects.
  • Removing the zero point mass can underestimate lfsr when genuine null effects are present.
What the authors say about other methods 38
  • Average sign-error probabilities and s-values parallel FDR estimates and Storey q-values, with lfdr substituted for lfsr recovering their FDR analogues.
  • Ash uses effect estimates and standard errors where locfdr and mixfdr use z scores and qvalue uses p-values, building on Wakefield’s analogous use of two-number summaries for Bayes factors.
  • Common parametric shrinkage priors obey unimodality but are less flexible than the general unimodal prior family proposed here.
  • The authors describe Cordy and Thomas deconvolution as containing the outlined approach apart from the zero point mass and its penalty, with a focus on estimating g rather than individual effects.
  • The unconstrained NPMLE used by Jiang and Zhang and Koenker and Mizera can relax unimodality but induces discrete posteriors whose uncertainty representation may require regularization.
  • The likelihood can be generalized from a normal density to a location-scale Student t density.
  • For alpha=1, ash.n lfsr values are monotone in p-values, generalizing Wakefield’s p-value-prior ranking result.
  • Fitting the scaled-effects model reduces to the alpha=0 algorithm applied to rescaled estimates and standard errors, followed by transforming the posterior back to beta_j.
  • The authors attribute holes near zero in locfdr and qvalue alternative distributions to treating near-zero z scores or near-one p-values as null, unlike the unimodal effect prior in ash.
  • Ash estimates mixture hyperparameters from the likelihood and plugs them into conditional effect posteriors.
  • The basic ash sampling model is the independent normal means likelihood with observation-specific estimated standard errors.
  • Ash uses a normal or t likelihood approximation based on two-number effect summaries.
  • Ash represents the prior as a point mass at zero and a mixture of fixed component distributions.
  • The basic ash prior mixes a point mass at zero with zero-centered normal distributions across a fixed scale grid.
  • The uniform-mixture variants use representations linked to classical characterizations of unimodal distributions.
  • For normal components with a normal likelihood the component posterior is normal.
  • The ash extension replaces the normal likelihood with a location-scale Student t likelihood.
  • Ash solves its convex penalized mixture-weight objective with interior-point methods.
  • Ash implements EM as an alternative optimizer for mixture weights.
  • The authors accelerate the EM algorithm using SQUAREM.
  • Ash uses a penalty based on a Dirichlet density to encourage conservative null-mass estimates.
  • Ash uses local FDR to summarize posterior null probabilities.
  • Ash s-values parallel Storey q-values; substituting local FDR for local false sign rate recovers the q-value construction.
  • The authors motivate local false sign rates by earlier recommendations to focus on sign confidence and type S errors.
  • Ash explicitly builds on Wakefield in using effect estimates and standard errors for inference.
  • The alpha=1 normal-mixture ash ranking result generalizes Wakefield p-value-prior ranking.
  • The authors identify the outlined ash construction with the elements of Cordy and Thomas except for the zero point mass and corresponding penalty.
  • The prior family can arbitrarily accurately approximate normal scale mixtures, including priors used by earlier wavelet EB methods and the horseshoe prior.
  • Ash uses a Gaussian normal-means sampling model with known potentially unequal errors.
  • The EB building block estimates its prior by marginal maximum likelihood before computing posteriors.
  • The ash prior family used here is a finite zero-centered Gaussian scale mixture.
  • The adopted scale-mixture family includes the prior distributions used by Clyde and George (2000).
  • The adopted scale-mixture family includes the prior distributions used by Johnstone and Silverman (2005b).
  • Fixed-grid mixture-weight optimization can use Convex optimization for empirical Bayes rules.
  • Fixed-grid mixture-weight optimization can use Mixture-proportion sequential quadratic programming.
  • Fixed-grid mixture-weight optimization can use Accelerated EM.
  • Accelerated EM is a stated alternative for fitting mixture weights.
  • The described implementation fits ash using MOSEK through REBayes KWDual.

10 Sum of Single Effects regression (SuSiE)

Built on Bayesian variable selection regression. What is new: sparse regression written as a sum of single effects.

Parts and other names of this method

  • ser part of this method
    single effect regression: the L = 1 building block

The problem it answers

  • Fine-mapping requires computationally practical Bayesian variable selection whose uncertainty summaries are easy to interpret.
  • Single-effect fine-mapping needs tractable uncertainty summaries that can retain correlated candidate variables together in a credible set.
  • Fine-mapping must estimate multiple-regression effects and the constituent SuSiE single-effect vectors from summary data.
  • Single-causal-variant fine-mapping needs analytically tractable posterior computations.

What it is

Model
y = X sum_l b_l + e; e ~ N(0, sigma^2 I_n)
Prior
L single-effect vectors; gamma_l ~ Mult(1, pi); scalar effects ~ N(0, sigma_0l^2); variances may differ
Fitting
IBSS residual SER updates; coordinate ascent over product_l q_l(b_l); optional variance updates by ELBO maximization
Reports
Approximate PIPs; per-component level-rho credible sets; variational posterior effect summaries
Data
Individual-level response y and predictor matrix X; centered variables
You set
L; target credible level rho; purity threshold (paper: 0.5); fixed or estimated residual and prior variances; fixed inclusion probabilities pi; initialization; ELBO increment stopping tolerance delta (paper: 0.001)

    one-effect linear regression
Assumes 4
  • The response and each explanatory-variable column are centered to mean zero, removing the intercept.
  • The SER errors are independent Gaussian errors with a shared residual variance.
  • Each SER effect vector has exactly one nonzero coordinate, whose location is determined by a one-hot selector.
  • The inclusion probabilities pi must be fixed and known, while uniform probabilities are adopted for simplicity.
Guarantees and stated results 10
  • The ELBO-maximizing update of one factor q_l, holding the others fixed, equals the posterior of a single effect regression fitted to the expected residuals, so each IBSS step is a coordinate ascent step on the ELBO. theorem
  • Selecting variables in decreasing posterior-probability order until cumulative mass reaches rho gives a smallest-cardinality level-rho SER credible set. theorem
  • IBSS performs coordinate ascent on the ELBO, equivalently coordinate descent on KL divergence within the factorized family. theorem
  • Under positive finite variance scales and strictly positive inclusion priors, the IBSS iterates converge to a stationary limit point of the ELBO. theorem
  • Identical predictor columns with equal inclusion priors have an exchangeable IBSS approximate posterior. theorem
  • For the general additive Gaussian model, a joint component posterior-and-prior update maximizing the ELBO equals optimization for the single-component model on expected residuals. theorem
  • At an exact single-component ELBO maximizer, the expected log prior-to-posterior ratio is given by the component marginal log-likelihood plus Gaussian normalization and expected-residual terms. theorem
  • For fixed L and p tending to infinity, the SuSiE prior and the standard prior selecting L distinct variables assign asymptotically equal probabilities to any event. theorem
  • The exact SER posterior has multinomial inclusion probabilities and conditional normal effects computable from marginal least-squares estimates and their variances. theorem
  • Under the direct RSS likelihood, SER inference does not depend on correlations between SNPs.
Stated limits 3
  • Variables absent from all reported credible sets may still have nonzero effects.
  • Bayesian 95% credible sets are not guaranteed to have 95% frequentist coverage.
  • IBSS can converge to poor local optima in change-point settings, and convergence problems also occur with many effect variables.
What the authors say about other methods 28
  • With L equal to one, the SuSiE model recovers the SER model.
  • IBSS replaces the single best-variable selections of forward stagewise selection with SER distributions over variable choices.
  • Unlike previous fully factorized BVSR variational approximations, the SuSiE factors can capture dependencies among variables within each single effect.
  • Lasso and elastic-net penalized likelihood select a best combination rather than quantify uncertainty among alternative variable combinations.
  • Estimating component prior variances can shrink extra single effects to zero, in a manner related to automatic relevance determination.
  • The additive SER construction suggests connections to boosting but uses model-averaged weak learners and backfitting with a Bayesian variational interpretation.
  • The Gaussian simple-regression Bayes factor matches the asymptotic Bayes-factor expression but is exact when the residual variance is given.
  • The at-least-one-effect credible-set definition differs from sets targeting all effect variables and is closer to signal clusters and minimal true detection.
  • Imposing a hierarchy on variables can restrict the reportable groups and force larger groups than supported by the data.
  • The authors do not expect substantial improvements over existing genetic prediction and heritability methods because the best existing approaches allow nonsparse effects.
  • SuSiE extends SER to multiple effects by adding single-effect vectors.
  • SuSiE builds on earlier Bayesian variable selection in regression.
  • SuSiE uses Gaussian multiple linear regression with coefficients represented as a sum of single effects.
  • SER is multiple regression restricted to exactly one nonzero regression coefficient.
  • IBSS updates each effect by fitting SER given the current estimates of other effects.
  • SER posterior computations use the p univariate regressions of the response on each predictor.
  • SER inclusion probabilities normalize prior-weighted simple-regression Bayes factors.
  • IBSS optimizes a variational approximation to the SuSiE posterior.
  • IBSS is coordinate ascent maximizing the ELBO over the stated factorized variational family.
  • The empirical Bayes version of SuSiE estimates the prior variances, effectively estimating the number of effects.
  • SER can estimate its prior and residual variances by marginal maximum likelihood before computing its posterior.
  • Hyperparameter estimation by ELBO maximization can be viewed as EM with an approximate E-step.
  • IBSS revisits earlier selections in light of later selections, as in backfitting.
  • SER credible sets use the procedure described by Maller et al. (2012).
  • SuSiE is a special case of the additive effects model with component mean X times a single-effect coefficient vector.
  • SER is the L = 1 special case of SuSiE, imposing exactly one causal SNP in the region.
  • SER is a multiple regression model constrained to exactly one nonzero coefficient.
  • The SER posterior inclusion probabilities normalize prior weights multiplied by single-SNP Bayes factors.

11 SMoothing by Adaptive SHrinkage

Built on Adaptive shrinkage (ash) and wavelet transform. What is new: ash applied to wavelet coefficients for smoothing.

Parts and other names of this method

  • poisson multiscale part of this method
    Poisson version in the same paper

The problem it answers

  • The method addresses heteroskedastic Gaussian mean and variance denoising and Poisson denoising underserved by existing EB approaches.
  • Shrinking multiscale split probabilities toward one half provides a way to estimate a spatially structured Poisson mean.

What it is

Model
Independent heteroskedastic Gaussian observations; Poisson branch uses recursive binomial splitting.
Prior
Resolution-specific zero-centered Gaussian scale mixture fitted by ash to multiscale parameters.
Fitting
Translation-invariant marginal ash shrinkage; inverse reconstruction; alternate mean and variance updates when both unknown; Gaussian working likelihood for variance stage.
Reports
Smoothed Gaussian mean and variance functions; Poisson intensity function via the multiscale branch.
Data
One-dimensional ordered Gaussian observations or Poisson counts; dyadic development, with equally spaced positions for direct application.
You set
Fixed component-scale grid; wavelet basis; the reported unknown-variance procedure uses two update cycles; no manually selected primary resolution level.

Assumes 5
  • The original Gaussian observation model assumes independent errors through its diagonal covariance matrix.
  • Both the mean function and variance function are assumed spatially structured.
  • For convenience, the multiscale development assumes a power-of-two signal length.
  • The posterior reconstruction exploits independence of split fractions across different scales.
  • The Poisson-to-binomial splitting construction assumes independent Poisson observations.
Guarantees and stated results 1
  • Two thirds of the fourth residual power is an unbiased estimator of the variance of the squared residual.
Stated limits 4
  • The marginal EB strategy accounts for unequal wavelet variances but ignores correlations among coefficients.
  • The method approximates transformed squared residuals by Gaussians despite their chi-square origin and may oversmooth rapidly varying variance functions.
  • Convergence of the alternating procedure is not guaranteed; two complete update cycles were accurate in the authors simulations.
  • Smash does not immediately apply to unequally spaced, non-power-of-two data; the authors treat uneven observations as equally spaced.
What the authors say about other methods 17
  • Unlike point-mass-at-one-half plus Beta priors used by Kolaczyk and Timmermann and Nowak, this approach uses ash to shrink log-odds parameters toward zero.
  • Smash extends the homoskedastic EB wavelet denoising ideas of Johnstone and Silverman to heteroskedastic Gaussian and Poisson problems using ash.
  • Smash uses ash for heteroskedastic shrinkage.
  • Smash follows resolution-specific EB shrinkage from Johnstone and Silverman.
  • Smash first wavelet-transforms the Gaussian observations.
  • Smash applies wavelet shrinkage to squared deviations to estimate variance.
  • Smash uses translation-invariant wavelet denoising by averaging circular shifts.
  • The implementation uses efficient wavelet algorithms rather than naive matrix multiplication.
  • The squared-deviation variance construction is stated to be similar to Delouille et al. (2004).
  • The squared-deviation variance construction is stated to be similar to Cai and Wang (2008).
  • The Poisson branch uses the multiscale representation from Kolaczyk (1999).
  • The Poisson branch uses the multiscale representation from Timmermann and Nowak (1999).
  • The Poisson branch uses the multiscale representation from Nowak and Kolaczyk (2000).
  • The Poisson branch applies ash to the multiscale parameters.
  • Poisson shrinkage inputs use log-odds estimates and standard errors based on Gart and Zweifel.
  • Poisson reconstruction approximates posterior split-probability moments with the delta method.
  • The Poisson TI-table construction follows Kolaczyk and ports its MATLAB implementation.

12 fSuSiE

Built on Sum of Single Effects regression (SuSiE) and Wavelet-based genetic association analysis and SMoothing by Adaptive SHrinkage. What is new: SuSiE for functional traits.

Parts and other names of this method

  • sfr part of this method
    single function regression: the one-effect building block
  • simple bfr part of this method
    one-covariate functional regression used inside SFR

The problem it answers

  • Single-trait fine-mapping and univariate SNP–trait tests do not adequately distinguish causal variants or exploit coordinated effects on nearby molecular traits.
  • Functional single-effect modeling must represent one covariate affecting an entire molecular profile rather than a scalar outcome.
  • Functional effect estimation needs shrinkage in wavelet space that induces spatial correlation on effects in the original space.

What it is

Model
Multiple wavelet regression D = X F + E with independent homoscedastic Gaussian residuals
Prior
Sum of R single-function effects with adaptive normal-mixture wavelet priors
Fitting
IBSS updates of single functions with a factorized variational posterior
Reports
SNP posterior inclusion probabilities
Data
Matched individual-level molecular-trait and genotype matrices
You set
Rmax; IS or SPS prior; mixture grid K and variances; pointwise interval level; optional purity filtering

8 LDpred

Built on spike-and-slab prior. What is new: point-normal prior for polygenic prediction from summary statistics.

Parts and other names of this method

  • ldpred2 version
    Same point-normal GWAS-and-LD regression and Gibbs posterior-mean fitting; grid implementation retains the LDpred method.
  • bpred part of this method
    the no-LD case described in the LDpred paper
  • ldpred2 auto part of this method
    LDpred2 option: causal fraction and heritability estimated in the sampler
  • ldpred2 sparse part of this method
    LDpred2 option: effects allowed to be exactly zero
  • ldpred inf part of this method
    the infinitesimal option (every variant causal)

The problem it answers

  • Pruning discards informative markers and failure to account for linked markers can bias effect estimates, limiting P+T regardless of its thresholds.
  • Genotype-based genomic BLUP and its non-infinitesimal extensions cannot be applied when only GWAS summary statistics are available.
  • A non-infinitesimal mixture model is motivated by the expectation that most traits do not follow the all-causal infinitesimal model.
  • The LDpred-inf special case allows analytical posterior mean effects and provides a computationally efficient version of LDpred.
  • LDpred2 addresses instability of LDpred in long-range LD regions and sensitivity to model misspecification at large GWAS sample sizes.
  • The auto extension estimates p and h2 within the model to remove the need for a validation dataset for hyperparameter selection.
  • The sparse extension is designed to produce estimates exactly equal to zero rather than the tiny nonzero estimates produced by LDpred1.
  • Polygenic scoring requires deriving joint predictive effects using summary statistics and LD information.

Assumes 16
  • The phenotype and each genetic variant are assumed mean centered and standardized to variance one.
  • The environmental and noise contribution is assumed independent of the genetic contribution.
  • Marker effects are assumed independently and identically drawn from the stated point-normal mixture.
  • The reference panel is required to match the population supplying the summary statistics, with mismatch potentially compromising prediction accuracy.
  • Summary statistics are assumed appropriately corrected for genetic ancestry; violations can mislead accuracy assessment or reduce prediction.
  • Absence of family and population structure in the training sample is invoked to justify an approximately banded LD matrix and local LD adjustment.
  • The regional approximation assumes small heritability explained by the region and negligible LD with SNPs outside the region.
  • The no-LD derivation assumes independent samples and unlinked genetic markers.
  • The aggregate heritability moment calculation assumes absence of population structure and independent identically distributed mean-zero SNP effects.
  • The derivation assumes known training LD, replaced in practice by representative reference LD; panels of at least 1,000 individuals were adequate in the reported simulations.
  • The displayed marginal-effect identity assumes the single-variant GWAS has no covariates.
  • Neglecting the fitted marginal effect in the residual-variance approximation requires that the marginal effect be small.
  • Replacing covariate-residualized variances by raw variances assumes that covariate effects are small.
  • The auto update assumes a binomial model for the number of nonzero effects given M and p.
  • Local LD modeling assumes correlations with variants beyond the chosen window are zero.
  • The QC underlying LDpred2-auto aims to ensure that external GWAS effects transfer to the target data.
Guarantees and stated results 5
  • The posterior mean prediction minimizes prediction error variance under the model.
  • The Bayesian prediction is correctly calibrated when the effect prior and LD modeling are correct.
  • The authors state that LDpred prediction accuracy converges to SNP-explained heritability as sample size grows, unlike P+T.
  • The expected marginal chi-squared statistic equals 1+N h_g^2 l_j/M under the stated moment assumptions.
  • The posterior mean approaches the maximum-likelihood estimator as training sample size increases.
Stated limits 11
  • An excessively large LD radius can introduce spurious distal LD and poor convergence, whereas too small a radius omits genuine LD.
  • The point-normal mixture may poorly represent genetic architecture, and another prior can perform better in some settings.
  • Fitting all markers simultaneously using raw genotypes may outperform methods based on marginal summary statistics.
  • Heterogeneity across cohorts may hinder prediction accuracy.
  • The analysis focuses on common variants and available LD panels are likely inadequate for rare variants.
  • Approximate Gibbs sampling can have robustness issues, with sensitivity to inaccurate LD estimates especially at very large training sample sizes.
  • Using validation data for reference LD can introduce small bias in individual prediction-accuracy estimation, while the authors regard it as valid for cohort prediction without case-control labels.
  • The authors did not derive a Bayesian estimator of h2 because of complexity.
  • A common genome-wide genetic-effect model may be misspecified when chromosome-specific architectures differ.
  • The genotype-standard-deviation approximation can fail for summary statistics from external-study meta-analysis.
  • LDpred2-auto can underperform despite summary-statistic quality control.
What the authors say about other methods 40
  • The aggregate heritability estimator is equivalent to LD-score regression with intercept constrained to one and inverse-LD-score weights.
  • LDpred-inf is a special case of LDpred and extends genomic BLUP to summary statistics through effects approximating genomic BLUP.
  • The posterior mode under a Laplace prior is the LASSO estimate.
  • LDpred resembles Gauss-Seidel but samples a posterior update rather than replacing the effect by its posterior mean.
  • LDpred shares a point-normal mixture prior with the cited Bayesian variable-selection study, while other cited approaches use mixtures of normals.
  • LDpred, BSLMM and BayesR model non-infinitesimal architectures, but BSLMM and BayesR require full genotypes.
  • MultiBLUP uses full genotypes and an infinitesimal prior that varies across regions, representing a different modeling extension.
  • LDpred explicitly conditions on sample size and accounts for the noise term under its model, unlike the contrasted joint-effect analysis.
  • The authors expect little or no gain from individual genotypes when true training LD is used and no unmodeled long-range LD remains.
  • The authors report generally more robust MCMC than variational Bayes results for summary statistics and suggest approximate LD as a possible reason.
  • The phenotype model uses an additive multiple linear regression on marker genotypes.
  • LDpred uses marginal least-squares marker effects from the additive phenotype model.
  • The non-infinitesimal prior uses a zero spike and Gaussian slab.
  • LDpred numerically approximates the posterior mean with an approximate MCMC Gibbs sampler.
  • LDpred uses Rao-Blackwellization to accelerate Gibbs-sampler convergence.
  • LDpred contains LDpred-inf as its Gaussian-infinitesimal special case.
  • LDpred has an analytic point-normal posterior-mean special case without LD, named Bpred.
  • LDpred-inf extends genomic BLUP to summary statistics with effects approximating genomic BLUP.
  • The Gaussian all-causal prior is the infinitesimal model.
  • The Gaussian-prior and Gaussian-summary-likelihood posterior is derived analytically by completing the square.
  • The LDpred posterior uses a joint Gaussian sampling density for marginal effect estimates conditional on effects and LD.
  • The linked-marker derivation follows Yang et al. for the LD-adjusted joint least-squares identity.
  • The unlinked Gaussian-infinitesimal posterior-mean building block is attributed to Dudbridge.
  • LDpred selects the causal-fraction prior by prediction accuracy in an independent validation dataset.
  • LDpred2 replaces the short physical-distance LD window with a genetic-distance window to capture long-range LD more efficiently.
  • Scaling effects by inverse genotype standard deviation as in LDpred1 is correct only when phenotypic variance equals one.
  • LDpred2-grid contains an infinitesimal model at p=1.
  • LDpred2 is a revised implementation of LDpred with improved robustness and computational efficiency.
  • LDpred2-auto extends LDpred by estimating p and h2 within the model.
  • The sparse option extends LDpred by allowing estimated effects to be exactly zero.
  • The marginal-to-joint effect derivation starts with joint linear regression on all variants and an intercept.
  • The derivation uses single-variant GWAS regression effects as marginal inputs.
  • The effect prior is a mixture of a point mass at zero and a zero-mean normal slab.
  • LDpred2 estimates effects using the Gibbs sampler inherited from LDpred.
  • The LDpred2-grid heritability grid is centered on a constrained LD score regression estimate.
  • LDpred2-auto uses the constrained LD score regression heritability estimate to initialize h2.
  • LDpred2-auto updates the causal proportion using a binomial count model with a beta prior and beta posterior.
  • The LDpred2 grid model contains the infinitesimal model when p equals one.
  • The authors use the Woodbury formula to express the joint effects after centering.
  • Binary-trait input quality control uses a genotype-standard-deviation approximation for summary statistics from logistic regression.

9 PRS-CS

Built on global-local shrinkage. What is new: continuous shrinkage prior for polygenic prediction.

Parts and other names of this method

  • prscs auto part of this method
    option: the global shrinkage scale is learned from the data instead of tuned

The problem it answers

  • Discrete-mixture priors create computational difficulties and may adjust local LD inaccurately, motivating a tractable continuous-shrinkage approach.
  • Global shrinkage needs to be learned from the data without reserving a validation data set for parameter selection.

What it is

Model
Standardized additive Gaussian phenotype model y=Z beta+epsilon; independent epsilon ~ N(0,sigma2 I); Jeffreys residual variance prior.
Prior
Independent gamma-gamma local scales; Gaussian effects with variance (sigma2/N) phi psi_j; a=1, b=1/2 (Strawderman-Berger). Global phi chosen by validation.
Fitting
Gibbs sampler with multivariate Gaussian effect updates within LD blocks and analytic full conditional updates for scales.
Reports
Posterior mean SNP effect sizes used as additive PRS weights.
Data
GWAS marginal least-squares effects, GWAS sample size and external blockwise LD; standardized model also accepts individual-level data.
You set
a=1; b=1/2; rho=1 minimum regularization; LD partition (1703 blocks in study); MCMC length and burn-in (1000/500 in simulations, 10000/5000 in application); validation grid sqrt(phi) in {0.0001,0.001,0.01,0.1,1}

Where it sits in STATO

  • breeding value estimation using genotype data broader
    a polygenic score is the human-genetics analogue of a genomic breeding value
  • Not in STATO
    no STATO term for clumping and thresholding
Assumes 7
  • Summing effects after clumping relies on retained SNPs being largely independent and their effects additive.
  • Overlap between base and target samples must be eliminated because it can substantially inflate target-trait association.
  • The described GWAS effect estimate assumes an additive effect per unit increase in genotype.
  • The described cross-trait analysis constructs base-phenotype scores in an independent target data set.
  • SNP effect sizes are assumed Gaussian in the simulation comparison.
  • Residual effects are assumed Gaussian in the simulation comparison.
  • All causal SNPs are included in the simulated dataset.
Guarantees and stated results 4
  • The authors state that permutation empirical P-values can support testing associations with optimized scores while maintaining appropriate type I error despite score overfitting.
  • The authors state that error-free population SNP effect estimates would allow target phenotype prediction with variance explained equal to chip heritability.
  • The permutation results support a 0.004 threshold for a false-positive rate below 0.05 in the studied design; the authors provisionally recommend 0.001.
  • The authors state that empirical association P-values control Type 1 error by repeating parameter optimization under the null.
Stated limits 13
  • The correlation cutoff used to remove SNPs in LD is typically arbitrary and remains a target for methodological development.
  • Correlated base-target differences in allele frequencies and environmental risks can generate spurious score associations even after perfect population-structure control in the base GWAS.
  • Separate base and target data do not by themselves provide out-of-sample evaluation when tuning uses the target; final evaluation needs data independent of training.
  • Grid search approximates the best-fit PRS; the authors state that identifying the true best fit requires testing every possible threshold.
  • Selecting the best-fit score entails multiple tests and inflates its unadjusted association significance.
  • The authors argue that correlated threshold-specific tests make Bonferroni correction by the number of tests overly conservative.
  • Best-guess genotype scoring does not account for uncertainty in the imputed genotype.
  • The authors recommend an independent validation sample to avoid overfitting, while noting that such a sample may be unavailable.
  • The observed variance explained remains unadjusted and affected by overfitting despite empirical P-value calibration.
  • Predictive accuracy requires out-of-sample prediction or cross-validation, with out-of-sample prediction preferred because of generalizability concerns.
  • The authors restrict the performance comparison to an approximate guide for settings matching their simulation assumptions.
  • The authors state that C+T does not appear to fully optimize predictive accuracy, while its simpler and typically smaller SNP set aids interpretation.
  • Standard PRS results require careful interpretation in family data or across diverse populations, and extensions or alternatives may be required.
What the authors say about other methods 16
  • Threshold-based scoring can be viewed as forward selection in GWAS P-value order with block updates determined by threshold increments.
  • Unlike random LD thinning, clumping preferentially selects trait-associated SNPs and can retain multiple independent effects within a region.
  • The guide distinguishes summary-statistic PRS from individual-level-only joint estimation and prediction approaches such as BLUP and LASSO.
  • The paper attributes the first application of the described cross-trait PRS technique to the International Schizophrenia Consortium (2009).
  • PRSice-2 uses the same standard clumping and P-value thresholding approach as PRSice.
  • In the reported simulations, PRSice-2 generally has higher predictive power than LDpred while the authors describe their power as comparable.
  • In the reported simulations, PRSice-2 generally has lower predictive power than lassosum while the authors describe their power as comparable.
  • PRSice-2 is a major overhaul of the original PRSice software and retains its C+T approach.
  • PRSice-2 uses LD- and P-value-based SNP clumping followed by P-value thresholding.
  • PRSice-2 incorporates code from PLINK-1.9 to optimize computation.
  • PRSice-2 permutes target phenotypes and repeats the PRS analysis to obtain an empirical association P-value.
  • PRSice-2 adds one to the empirical-P-value numerator and denominator, citing North et al. for the observed-configuration correction.
  • The authors require out-of-sample prediction or cross-validation to evaluate PRSice-2 predictive accuracy.
  • PRSice-2 uses linear regression on dummy-coded PRS strata to estimate quantitative-trait differences from the reference stratum.
  • PRSice-2 uses logistic regression to estimate relative risk for PRS strata compared with the reference stratum.
  • PRSice-2 can use externally imputed BGEN genotype inputs and convert them to best-guess genotypes or dosages for scoring.

  • uses marginal GWAS regression when Marginal effect estimates, allele frequencies and representative reference-panel covariance are available.
    Stage 1 reconstructs the linear-model cross-product from marginal GWAS maximum-likelihood effects and allele frequencies, with covariance from a representative reference panel.
    “XTy can be calculated from the vector of maximum likelihood marginal effects, 𝛃 ^, available from GWAS summary statistics by ( X^{T} y )_{i} = 2 n 𝛉_{i} ( 1 − 𝛉_{i} ) 𝛃 ^_{i}, where n is the sample size, θ is the vector of allele frequencies and ( X^{T} y )_{i} is the ith element of XTy, with i indexing SNPs. XTX = nΦ; here, Φ is the pairwise genotypic covariance, which can be estimated from a reference panel representative of the population used in the GWAS. Thus, rescaling λ by n, the posterior is estimated as”

Where it sits in STATO

  • breeding value estimation using genotype data broader
    as above
  • ridge regression best linear unbiaised predictor close
    per-locus Gaussian prior, stated equivalent to ridge regression
  • prior probability distribution broader
    the population-1 posterior is used as a prior
  • posterior probability distribution broader
    the population-1 posterior is used as a prior
  • Not in STATO
    no STATO term for transferring a posterior across populations
Assumes 4
  • The locus-level models assume each locus is independent of every other locus.
  • Reference-panel genotypic covariance is estimated from a panel representative of the GWAS population.
  • For incomplete SNP overlap, stage 2 uses the intersection and conditions the prior on nonoverlapping effects being zero.
  • The first-order F-statistic approximation assumes the locus-explained variance term is small.
Guarantees and stated results 2
  • As tau tends to infinity, the stage-2 effects approach the population-1 effects, according to the stated limiting interpretation.
  • When the variance explained by a locus is small, a first-order Taylor approximation gives the displayed quadratic approximation to the F statistic.
Stated limits 2
  • The pseudo-F tail probability cannot be interpreted as a P value because the parameter estimates include prior information.
  • The authors expect improved BridgePRS performance when contributing GWAS effect estimates are on the same scale.
What the authors say about other methods 19
  • The discovery-population zero-centered Gaussian locus model is equivalent to penalized-likelihood ridge regression.
  • The authors contrast PRS-CSx sharing shrinkage information across ancestries with BridgePRS sharing effect-size information.
  • In the reported simulations, BridgePRS performs better relative to PRS-CSx as uncertainty increases through lower power, higher polygenicity, greater diversity or missing causal variants.
  • BridgePRS averages effects across variants within a locus rather than selecting the single best variant as clumping and thresholding does.
  • The locus model uses a Gaussian linear trait likelihood with a multivariate Gaussian SNP-effect prior.
  • Stage 1 uses Gaussian conjugacy to obtain SNP-effect posterior distributions analytically.
  • Stage 2 also uses a conjugate Gaussian posterior update.
  • The stage combines candidate genome-wide PRSs using ridge regression fitted to test data.
  • The stage combines candidate genome-wide PRSs using ridge regression fitted to test data.
  • Leave-one-out cross-validation selects the ridge shrinkage parameter to minimize out-of-sample deviance.
  • BridgePRS uses glmnet to fit the cross-validated ridge combination of candidate PRSs.
  • Stage 1 reconstructs the linear-model cross-product from marginal GWAS maximum-likelihood effects and allele frequencies, with covariance from a representative reference panel.
  • Stage 2 updates discovery-derived effects using target GWAS summaries, including marginal maximum-likelihood SNP effects, allele frequencies and locus covariance.
  • BridgePRS adopts allele-frequency-dependent SNP-effect prior precision, citing Speed et al. (2012).
  • The stage-2 pseudo-F ranking adapts the linear-regression F test by substituting posterior quantities and a prior-adjusted effective sample size.
  • BridgePRS defines loci by clumping and thresholding GWAS summaries using ancestry-matched LD.
  • BridgePRS uses PLINK v.1.9 to clump GWAS summary statistics when defining loci.
  • BridgePRS cites Fong and Holmes for approximating linear-regression marginal likelihood from cross-validated residual variance to weight candidate models.
  • The final PRS averages three candidate PRSs using posterior model weights computed from marginal likelihoods and equal prior model weights.
